newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Four arrested in Argentine Jewish cemetery attack.
newsitem.headline: Four arrested in Argentine Jewish cemetery attack.

text.p: Argentine police on Thursday arrested four men suspected of attacking a Jewish cemetery last week, smashing and marking 100 tombstones with swastikas.

Judge Victor Termite told reporters the men were arrested during overnight raids in the Buenos Aires outskirts in which pamphlets and documents also were seized, although he declined to comment on their content.
The suspects claimed to belong to nationalistic organisations that Jewish community members said were well-known right-wing, anti-Semitic groups.

The incident, the latest in a spate of attacks in the past few years that included two major bomb blasts and at least five cemetery desecrations, has triggered protests by Jewish and human rights groups and by political parties.

Bet El, a leading Argentine Jewish group, on Tuesday blamed "nazis in the state's repressive apparatus" for the attacks, calling the local Jewish community "the most vulnerable in the world." Argentina's best-known human rights group, the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo, demonstrated against the incidents outside the government house on Thursday.
A car bomb razed the Israeli Embassy in 1992, killing 29 people, and another one destroyed the main Jewish community centre in Buenos Aires in 1994, killing 86.

Argentine security services have been criticised by the Jewish community, Israel and the United States for failing to find the authors of the bomb attacks, which have been blamed on the Iranian-backed Moslem fundamentalist Hizbollah group.

Argentina in the past gave shelter to notorious Nazis, including Holocaust architect Adolf Eichmann, Auschwitz death camp doctor Josef Mengele and Erich Priebke, now under trial in Rome for Italy's worst Second World War atrocity.
Last July, former Justice Minister Rodolfo Barra resigned after a magazine revealed he belonged to a Nazi group in his youth.
